hook.text: Every night, a warehouse rebuilds its models: the cleaned staging tables, the joins, the facts and dimensions that dashboards read. Each one is built from others, so they have to run in the right order.

hook-dbt.text: Working out that order, and running it, is dbt's job.

plan.text: Twenty questions on how it builds a project: ten worked through on the page's own models, and ten quick ones to finish.

what.text: Question one. What is dbt, and what does it actually do? It's the T in ELT: extract, load, transform. You write each transformation as a select statement, called a model, and dbt builds the models in order, inside your warehouse.

what-wrap.text: It decides how each result is stored, by wrapping your select in a create view or a create table, and it runs your tests and writes your docs alongside.

what-not.text: It doesn't move data: loading raw tables is the job of extract and load tools. What it adds is software practice for SQL: version control, modular models, tests, and continuous integration, or CI.
what-not.spoken: It doesn't move data: loading raw tables is the job of extract and load tools. What it adds is software practice for sequel: version control, modular models, tests, and continuous integration, or CI.

ref.text: Question two. What do ref and source do? Source points at a raw table that something else loaded, declared once by name. Ref points at another model.

ref-edges.text: Here the staging model reads raw orders through source, and the orders fact reads the staging model through ref. Each call tells dbt that one thing depends on another.

ref-hard.text: Hardcode the table name instead, and dbt no longer sees that dependency. Nothing stops it building the fact before the model it reads, and the lineage graph has a gap where the edge was.

dag.text: Question three. What is the dbt lineage DAG, and how is it built? DAG is short for directed acyclic graph. dbt parses every ref and source call in the project, and each call becomes an edge, from the node it names to the model that names it.
dag.spoken: Question three. What is the dbt lineage dag, and how is it built? Dag is short for directed acyclic graph. dbt parses every ref and source call in the project, and each call becomes an edge, from the node it names to the model that names it.

dag-order.text: The page's slice has two sources, four models and five edges. Both staging models depend only on sources, so they build side by side. The customer dimension waits for its staging model, and the orders fact for both branches: four models in three steps.

dag-acyclic.text: Acyclic is what makes an order possible. If two models referenced each other, neither could go first.

layers.text: Question four. How do staging, intermediate, and mart layers differ? Staging has one model per source table: renaming, typing and light cleaning, with no business logic. Intermediate holds reusable business logic: joins and reshaping. Marts are the finished facts and dimensions that dashboards read.

layers-dry.text: Each step stays small, testable, and written once.

layers-cost.text: The layers also decide what a change costs. Select a model with a plus after it, and dbt builds everything downstream. From the customers staging model, that's three of the four models, all the way to the revenue dashboard. From the orders fact, it's one.

layers-rule.text: So the business logic, which changes every week, sits downstream, in intermediate models and marts, where a change rebuilds less. Staging stays shaped like the source, which rarely changes.

mat.text: Question five. Compare the materializations: view, table, incremental, ephemeral.

mat-view.text: Take the page's customer dimension: one row per customer, grouped from twenty-four events. As a view, only the query is stored, so every read regroups all twenty-four. It's cheap to build, slower to read, and always current: a new customer's event shows up at once.

mat-table.text: As a table, the result is computed once per run. A read is twelve stored rows, which is fast, but the table misses that new customer until the next run, and every run recomputes everything.

mat-incr.text: Incremental keeps the table, and processes only new or changed rows on each run, for large tables that mostly append.

mat-eph.text: And ephemeral isn't stored at all.

mat-pick.text: Choose by read frequency, compute cost and data volume, not habit. An expensive model that dashboards read all day, from a source that changes nightly, should be a table.

eph.text: Question six. What is an ephemeral model, and when should you use it? dbt compiles it as a CTE, a common table expression, inside every model that refs it. Nothing is created in the warehouse.

eph-when.text: Use one for intermediate logic referenced once or twice. Referenced by many models, the same CTE is copied into each. And since it isn't a table, you can't query it or test it on its own.

build.text: Question seven. What is the difference between dbt run, dbt test, and dbt build? Run builds the models. Test runs the tests against models already built. Build does both, with seeds and snapshots too, in graph order: each model is tested as soon as it's built.

build-why.text: The order is the point. With run, then test, a broken staging model has already fed everything downstream before any test fails. Build tests a model before anything downstream of it is built, so a failure stops where it starts.

build-ci.text: That's why build is the command to run in CI.

subset.text: Question eight. How do you run only a subset of models in dbt? With the select flag on dbt run, followed by a model's name, a folder like marts, or a tag like nightly.

subset-alone.text: A model selected alone is rebuilt alone. Its parents are read as they already stand in your schema, and in a fresh development schema, they may not exist yet.

subset-plus.text: A plus in front adds everything upstream: put one before the orders fact, and all four models build, in order. A plus after adds everything downstream, which is how question four counted a change.

env.text: Question nine. What are environments and targets in dbt? A target is a named warehouse connection: the database, the schema and the credentials. Teams usually have two environments: dev, where each developer builds into their own schema, and prod.

env-ref.text: Ref resolves to the active target's schema. The same reference to the staging model reads Alice's schema in development and the production schema in the nightly job, with no code change.

env-hard.text: That's the other half of hardcoding a name. Written as the production table, it makes Alice's development run read production, not the model she just changed.

schema.text: Question ten. How do you handle environment-specific schemas in dbt? With the schema config, and the macro that turns it into a name: generate schema name.

schema-dev.text: By default, dbt adds a model's custom schema to the target's own. Alice's staging models land in dbt alice staging, so two developers never overwrite each other.

schema-prod.text: Production usually wants the plain name, staging, so teams customize the macro to drop the prefix there.

r-seeds.text: Question eleven. What are seeds in dbt? CSV files kept in the repository and loaded as tables by dbt seed: small reference data with no source system, like country codes. Nothing large, and nothing that changes often.

r-macros.text: Question twelve. How do macros work in dbt? A macro is a reusable Jinja function that writes SQL: cents to dollars emits amount cents over a hundred point oh, wherever it's called. Written once, it's right everywhere. Typed by hand over a plain hundred, Postgres divides integers, and nineteen ninety-nine cents becomes nineteen dollars.
r-macros.spoken: Question twelve. How do macros work in dbt? A macro is a reusable Jinja function that writes sequel: cents to dollars emits amount cents over a hundred point oh, wherever it's called. Written once, it's right everywhere. Typed by hand over a plain hundred, Postgres divides integers, and nineteen ninety-nine cents becomes nineteen dollars.

r-packages.text: Question thirteen. What are dbt packages, and how do you add one? Shared dbt projects of macros, models and tests. List one in packages dot YAML, pinned to a version, and run dbt deps. The most common is dbt utils.
r-packages.spoken: Question thirteen. What are dbt packages, and how do you add one? Shared dbt projects of macros, models and tests. List one in packages dot yammel, pinned to a version, and run dbt deps. The most common is dbt utils.

r-vars.text: Question fourteen. How do you pass variables into dbt models? Read one with var in the model, give it a default in the project file, and override it on the command line as JSON.
r-vars.spoken: Question fourteen. How do you pass variables into dbt models? Read one with var in the model, give it a default in the project file, and override it on the command line as jay-son.

r-exposures.text: Question fifteen. What are exposures in dbt? YAML entries for what reads your models: a dashboard, a machine learning model, a reverse ETL sync. They sit in the lineage graph, which is how question four's change reached the revenue dashboard.
r-exposures.spoken: Question fifteen. What are exposures in dbt? Yammel entries for what reads your models: a dashboard, a machine learning model, a reverse ETL sync. They sit in the lineage graph, which is how question four's change reached the revenue dashboard.

r-docs.text: Question sixteen. How does dbt manage documentation and lineage? dbt docs generate builds a site from the descriptions in YAML and markdown doc blocks, and dbt docs serve opens it, with an interactive graph drawn from the same ref and source calls.
r-docs.spoken: Question sixteen. How does dbt manage documentation and lineage? dbt docs generate builds a site from the descriptions in yammel and markdown doc blocks, and dbt docs serve opens it, with an interactive graph drawn from the same ref and source calls.

r-project.text: Question seventeen. What is the dbt project YAML file, and what does it control? The root configuration: the project's name, its folders, and default configs by folder, such as a materialization. A folder's setting overrides the project's, and a model's own config overrides both.
r-project.spoken: Question seventeen. What is the dbt project yammel file, and what does it control? The root configuration: the project's name, its folders, and default configs by folder, such as a materialization. A folder's setting overrides the project's, and a model's own config overrides both.

r-version.text: Question eighteen. How do you version a dbt model? Since dbt one point five, declare versions in YAML, each with its own SQL file. Consumers pin one with ref and a version number, so a breaking change rolls out without forcing everyone across at once.
r-version.spoken: Question eighteen. How do you version a dbt model? Since dbt one point five, declare versions in yammel, each with its own sequel file. Consumers pin one with ref and a version number, so a breaking change rolls out without forcing everyone across at once.

r-debug.text: Question nineteen. What is dbt debug, and when do you use it? It checks your connection setup: that the profiles file is valid, and that dbt can reach the warehouse. Run it on a new environment, or on a connection error, before you debug any model.

next.text: A table materialization recomputes everything on every run. For a billion-row table, every night, that's the cost incremental models cut. Next: incremental models.

r-v2.text: Question twenty. What is dbt v2, and how does it relate to dbt Core? It's the engine rewritten in Rust, generally available since September 2026: the main distribution is now just called dbt, and dbt Core names the Python one point x line, still supported, and ending at one point thirteen. It parses and type-checks your SQL, so a misspelled column is caught at compile time, and it validates YAML strictly, so every one point x deprecation warning has to be fixed first.
r-v2.spoken: Question twenty. What is dbt v2, and how does it relate to dbt Core? It's the engine rewritten in Rust, generally available since September 2026: the main distribution is now just called dbt, and dbt Core names the Python one point x line, still supported, and ending at one point thirteen. It parses and type-checks your sequel, so a misspelled column is caught at compile time, and it validates yammel strictly, so every one point x deprecation warning has to be fixed first.

env-profile.text: Each is a target in your profile, picked with the target flag, and the hosted dbt platform sets up the same split as environments.

r-version-latest.text: A ref with no version gets the latest version, which defaults to the highest number. So set latest version to one until consumers have moved.
